title: Windows Event Logs Deep Dive
description: Parse security, system, and application logs to reconstruct login events, process creation, and attacks.

slides.title: The Operating System's Journal 📓
slides.content:
# Windows Event Logs

Event logs are the primary source for system, security, and application events. They record logons, process starts, service installs, RDP connections, and much more.

Log formats:
- **.evt**: Legacy (Windows XP/2003).
- **.evtx**: Modern XML‑based (Vista+). Stored in `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs`.

Key log files:
- `Security.evtx`: Logon/logoff, account management, audit policy changes.
- `System.evtx`: Driver failures, service starts, system time changes.
- `Application.evtx`: Application errors and events.
- `Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager%4Operational.evtx`: RDP connections.

quizData.question: Which event log file contains logon and logoff events?
quizData.explanation: Security.evtx records audit events such as successful/failed logons, account changes, and policy modifications.

slides.title: Event IDs – The Decoder Ring 🔢
slides.content:
Each event has an **Event ID** and a source. Crucial IDs for forensics:

| Event ID | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| 4624 | Successful logon |
| 4625 | Failed logon |
| 4634 | Logoff |
| 4648 | Explicit logon (runas, scheduled tasks) |
| 4672 | Special privileges assigned (admin logon) |
| 4688 | Process creation (if audit enabled) |
| 7045 | Service installed |
| 1102 | Audit log cleared |
| 21 / 25 | RDP logon (TerminalServices) |

Logon type codes in 4624: 2 (console), 10 (RDP), 5 (service), 7 (unlock).

slides.title: Parse Evtx with EvtxECmd (Eric Zimmerman)
slides.content: Use EvtxECmd to dump all logs to CSV.

quizData.question: A logon type 10 in event 4624 indicates a logon via ___.
quizData.explanation: Type 10 is RemoteInteractive, used for RDP connections.

slides.title: Process Creation & Command Line 🖥️
slides.content:
If audit policy **Process Creation** is enabled (event 4688), you get the full command line of every process started. This is forensic gold – it shows what was executed, including malicious scripts.

Also, event 1 from `Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational` provides even richer process creation data if Sysmon is installed.

Check the `CommandLine` field in the event details.

quizData.question: Event ID 4688 is logged by default on all Windows systems without any additional configuration.
quizData.explanation: Process creation auditing must be enabled via Group Policy or local security policy; it's not on by default in many versions.

slides.title: RDP Connection Forensics 💻
slides.content:
The TerminalServices logs (Operational and Admin) hold RDP sessions. Event 21 and 25 show remote logon and reconnection, with source IP address.

`Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager/Operational` event 1149 records user authentication details.

These logs are essential for investigating lateral movement or unauthorized remote access.

quizData.question: Which event source is most useful for tracing RDP connections, including the client IP?
quizData.explanation: TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager records events 21,25 with source IP and username.

slides.title: Log Clearing & Tampering 🗑️
slides.content:
Event ID 1102 (Security) and 104 (System) indicate that the event log was cleared – a strong sign of anti‑forensics.

Always check for gaps in timestamps and compare the size of logs to expected activity. Attackers may use `wevtutil cl` to wipe logs.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use Timeline Explorer

Tools like Timeline Explorer (Eric Zimmerman) can visualize event logs in a single, filterable timeline along with other artifacts. It's a game‑changer for correlation.
